Random Variables

A random variable is a mapping that assigns a real number \(X(\omega)\) to each outcome \(\omega \in \Omega\).

\[X: \Omega \to \mathbb{R}\]

  • We say \(X\) is a discrete random variable if the domain is a set of integers. These are typically used when counting.
  • We say \(X\) is a continuous random variable if the domain is a continuous interval of real numbers. These are typically used when measuring.
Discrete Example

Let discrete random variable \(X\) denote the number of pop songs in a randomly selected playlist of 40 songs.

  • The sample space \(\Omega\) is all possible playlists of 40 songs (say picking with replacement).
  • An outcome \(\omega\) is one randomly selected playlist of 40 songs.
  • \(X\) maps each \(\omega\) to a value in the set of integers \(\left\{ 0, 1, 2, \ldots, 39, 40 \right\}\)
Continuous Example

Let continuous random variable \(X\) denote the weight (in ounces) of a randomly selected book from the library.

  • The sample space \(\Omega\) is all possible books in the library.
  • An outcome \(\omega\) is one book in the library.
  • \(X\) maps each \(\omega\) to a value in the interval \(( 0, \infty )\)

The Ecdat package contains a number of data sets related to economics and political science. If you have not already installed the package, be sure to run install.packages("Ecdat") in the console below. Then load the package by running the command below.

library(Ecdat)  # package with some econ data
library(tidyverse)
library(ggthemes)  # to access color palette and other themes

The Panel Study of Income Dynamics (PSID) is a long-running, nationally representative survey of U.S. families. It has followed the same families since 1968, gathering data on income, employment, wealth, housing, marriage, and other socioeconomic factors. The data in PSID is a subset (from 1993) of the full data set containing 4856 observations with 8 variables listed below:

Question 1: Probability Questions

According to US Census data, in 1993 the proportion of adults in the US that were married was 47%. What is the probability of picking a random sample of 50 adults in the US in 1993 that has exactly 25 married adults? At most 25 married adults? At least 25 married adults?

Tip

Use a binomial distribution! See the appendix for help using functions such as dbinom, pbinom, rbinom and/or qbinom.

Solution to Question 1

# dbinom(x, n, p) where n is sample size and
# p is prob of "success"
dbinom(25, 50, 0.47)  # exactly 25
[1] 0.1025951
pbinom(25, 50, 0.47)  # at most 25 includes 25
[1] 0.7149783
1 - pbinom(24, 50, 0.47) # at least 25 includes 25
[1] 0.3876168




Question 2: A Statistical Question

A random sample of 50 adults in the US in 1993 is randomly selected. If 24 out of the 50 adults in the sample are married, what is the proportion of all adults in the US in 1993 that are married?

Solution to Question 2

If the sample is picked randomly, then it should resemble the population. The proportion of the sample that is married (a statistic denoted \(\hat{p}\)), should be “close” to proportion of all US adults in 1993 that were married (a parameter denoted \(p\)).

Note

It is common to use “hat” notation to indicate something is an estimator for a parameter. The “hat” over the symbol means “an estimator for”. We denote the sample proportion \(\hat{p}\) (pronounced p-hat) since we use it to estimate the parameter \(p\).

Point Estimates

We have a sample proportion \(\hat{p} = \frac{24}{50} = 0.48\). Thus, a reasonable estimate is \(p \approx \hat{p} = 0.48\). When we estimate a population parameter with one value, this is called a point estimate. Two common methods for finding point estimates for a parameter given sample data are:

  • Maximum Likelihood Estimates (MLE) use probability methods and optimization.
  • Method of Moments (MoM) are a curving fitting approach that involves a system of non-linear equations.

Of course, sample statistics will vary. We might get another sample with the proportion married people equal to \(0.46\). A third sample might have \(0.49\) as the proportion of married people. They all should be “close” to the value of \(p\) (bias) Using the same method results in different point estimates. We consider various properties when deciding which estimator is best. Below some are some common properties to consider.

  • An estimator is unbiased if, on average, the estimate equals the value of the parameter, \(E \left( \hat{\theta} \right) = \theta\).
  • The efficiency is \(\text{Var}\left( \hat{\theta} \right)\) which measures the variability of the estimator.
  • The Mean Square Error (MSE) is a property to takes into account both the bias and variability of an estimator.
  • An estimator is consistent if its value converges to the value of the parameter as the sample size \(n \to \infty\).
Caution

If we pick a sample with 50 adults from a population with \(47\%\) that is married, we will never get a point estimate \(\hat{p} = 0.47\), so it is impossible to get a point estimate (using this method) that equals the actual value of parameter \(p\).

Interval Estimates

Rather than give a single value to estimate the population parameter, we often try to quantify the variability of the sample statistics (for example using the standard error of an underlying sampling distribution). Then we can build a margin of error into our estimate to account for this variability and give an interval estimate for the parameter. Confidence intervals are interval estimates that have the a specified success rate (confidence level) of containing the parameter. For example, a 95% confidence interval has a 95% chance of containing the actual value of the unknown population parameter.

  • For some statistics (such as means and proportions), we can theoretically model the underlying sampling distribution using the Central Limit Theorem (CTL) as long as certain conditions have been satisfied.
    • CLT only applies for a small number of statistics, means and proportions most commonly.
    • CLT gets more accurate as the sample size increases, and it may not apply if samples are not large enough.
  • We can almost always apply resampling methods such as bootstrapping to approximate a sampling distribution.
    • Resampling methods can be used to simulate sampling distributions for any statistic.
# using a Wald confidence interval with no continuity correction
p_hat <- 0.48  # point est is p = p_hat
se <- sqrt(0.48 * (1 - 0.48) / 50)  # compute standard error

# putting each calculation in parentheses prints to screen as well
(wald_low <- p_hat - 1.96 * se) 
[1] 0.341518
(wald_up <- p_hat + 1.96 * se)
[1] 0.618482

The interval from \(0.341\) to \(0.618\) has a 95% chance of containing the proportion of all adults in the US that were married in 1993.

# score confidence interval with a continuity correction
prop.test(24, 50, conf.level = 0.95)

    1-sample proportions test with continuity correction

data:  24 out of 50, null probability 0.5
X-squared = 0.02, df = 1, p-value = 0.8875
alternative hypothesis: true p is not equal to 0.5
95 percent confidence interval:
 0.3388090 0.6242435
sample estimates:
   p 
0.48

The interval from \(0.339\) to \(0.624\) has a 95% chance of containing the proportion of all adults in the US that were married in 1993.

We can use resampling methods to construct a Bootstrap Confidence Interval. We can represent our initial sample of \(n=50\) with 24 married adults as a vector of logicals. We have 24 TRUE entries and 26 FALSE entries stored in my_samp to represent our sample of adults

my_samp <- c(rep(TRUE, 24), rep(FALSE, 26))
my_samp
 [1]  TRUE  TRUE  TRUE  TRUE  TRUE  TRUE  TRUE  TRUE  TRUE  TRUE  TRUE  TRUE
[13]  TRUE  TRUE  TRUE  TRUE  TRUE  TRUE  TRUE  TRUE  TRUE  TRUE  TRUE  TRUE
[25] FALSE FALSE FALSE FALSE FALSE FALSE FALSE FALSE FALSE FALSE FALSE FALSE
[37] FALSE FALSE FALSE FALSE FALSE FALSE FALSE FALSE FALSE FALSE FALSE FALSE
[49] FALSE FALSE
mean(my_samp)  # sample proportion married adults
[1] 0.48
set.seed(101)  # set seed for fixed randomization
N <- 10^5  # Number of bootstrap samples
boot_prop <- numeric(N)  # create vector to store bootstrap proportions

# for loop that creates bootstrap dist
for (i in 1:N)
{
  x <- sample(my_samp, size = 50, replace = TRUE)  # pick a bootstrap resample
  boot_prop[i] <- mean(x)  # compute bootstrap sample proportion
}

(boot_low <- quantile(boot_prop, 0.025))  # lower cutoff
2.5% 
0.34 
(boot_up <- quantile(boot_prop, 0.975))  # upper cutoff
97.5% 
 0.62

The interval from \(0.34\) to \(0.62\) has a 95% chance of containing the proportion of all adults in the US that were married in 1993.

# plot bootstrap distribution
hist(boot_prop,  
     breaks=20, 
     xlab = "p-hat, sample proportion",
     main = "Bootstrap Distribution for Sample Proportion")

# blue lines at each cutoff
abline(v = boot_low, col = "blue", lwd = 2, lty = 2)
abline(v = boot_up, col = "blue", lwd = 2, lty = 2)

Probability Density Functions

If \(X\) is a discrete random variable, we define the probability mass function (pmf) for \(X\), denoted \(p_X(x)\), as the probability random variable \(X\) is exactly equal to \(x\), \(p_X(x) = P(X=x)\).

If \(X\) is a continuous random variable, we denote the probability density function (pdf) for \(X\) as \(f_X(x)\) and we interpret the value differently from the discrete case. The units of \(f_X(x)\) are proportion per unit of \(X\).

  • We compute probabilities from the pdf of a continuous random variable using areas under the graph of \(f_X(x)\).
  • We use definite integrals to compute probabilities from a pdf, \[P(a < X < b) = \int_a^b f_X(x) \, dx = \text{an area under } f_X(x).\]
Caution

Be careful to interpret the output of pdf’s and pmf’s differently. If \(X\) is a continuous random variable, the output of the pdf \(f_X(a)\) is NOT the probability that \(X=a\). The probability that a continuous random variable \(X\) is exactly equal to any value is 0, \(P(X = a) = 0\).

Example

Let continuous random variable \(X\) denote the height (in inches) of a randomly selected adult. Suppose we know \(f_X(70) = 0.02\).

  • The probability that a random person is exactly 70 inches is 0%. Thus \(P(X = 70) = 0\).
  • \(f_X(70) = 0.02\) tells us about 2% of the population is between \(69.5\) and \(70.5\) inches tall.

Cumulative Distribution Functions

If \(X\) is a random variable, we define the cumulative distribution function (cdf) as \(F_X(x)=P(X \leq x)\). It gives the proportion of all values less than or equal to \(x\).

  • For a discrete random variable, we sum: \[F_X(x) = P(X \leq x) = \sum_{k=\text{min value}}^x p_X(k).\]
  • For a continuous random variable, we integrate: \[F_X(x) = P(X \leq x) = \int_{-\infty}^x f_X(t) \, dt.\]
    • The cdf \(F_X(x)\) is an antiderivative of the pdf \(f_X(x)\).
    • The pdf is the derivative of the cdf.

Expected Value

The average or expected value for a discrete random variable \(X\) is denote \(E(X)\) or \(\mu_X\) and computed using the formulas below depending on whether the random variable \(X\) is discrete or continuous.

  • For a discrete random variable, we sum: \(\displaystyle E(X) = \mu_X = \sum_x \left( x \cdot p_X(x) \right)\).
  • For a continuous random variable, we integrate: \(\displaystyle E(X) = \mu_X = \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} x \cdot f_X(x) \, dx\).

Let \(X\) and \(Y\) denote two random variables and \(a\) and \(b\) denote two constants. Then we have:

Properties of Expected Value

  • \(E(a) = a\)

  • \(E(aX + bY) = aE(X) + bE(Y)\)

  • \(E(XY) = E(X)E(Y) + \text{Cov}(X, Y)\)

Variance and Standard Deviation

The variance for a discrete random variable \(X\) is one common way to measure how spread out (in relation to the expected value) are the values of \(X\). The variance is denoted \(\text{Var}(X)\) or \(\sigma^2_X\) and computed using the formulas:

\[\text{Var}(X) = \sigma^2_X = \sum_x \left( (x-\mu)^2 \cdot p_X(x) \right) \quad \text{or} \quad \text{Var}(X) = \sigma^2_X = \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} (x-\mu)^2 \cdot f_X(x) \, dx .\]

The standard deviation for a discrete random variable \(X\) is the square root of the variance and is denoted by \(\sigma_X\). It more or less measures the average of the distances for each value of \(X\) from the mean \(\mu\). \[\text{SD}(X) = \sigma_X = \sqrt{\text{Var}(X)} \]

Note

We often use the standard error instead of the variance when describing the spread of \(X\) since the standard deviation has the same units as \(X\) and is easier to interpret in practical terms.

Let \(X\) and \(Y\) denote two random variables and \(a\) denote a constant. Then we have:

Properties of Variance

  • \(\text{Var}(a) = 0\)

  • \(\text{Var}(aX) = a^2 \text{Var}(X)\)

  • \(\text{Var}(X) = E(X^2) - \big( E(X) \big)^2 = E(X^2) - \mu_X^2\)

  • \(\text{Var}(X + Y) = \text{Var}(X) \text{Var}(Y) + 2\text{Cov}(X,Y)\)

Question 3

Using properties of discrete random variables, show that for any discrete random variable \(X\) with pmf \(p(X)\) and expected value \(E(X) = \mu\), we have

\[\text{Var}(X) = E(X^2) - \mu^2.\]

Solution to Question 3

Finish the proof below!

Let \(X\) be a discrete random variable with pmf \(p(x)\) and expected value \(E(X)=\mu\). Then we have

\[\begin{array}{rcll} \text{Var}(X) &=& \sum_x \left( (x-\mu)^2 \cdot p(x) \right) & \text{(by definition)}\\ &=& \sum_x \left( (x^2 -2 \mu x + \mu^2) \cdot p(x) \right) & \text{(distributing squared term)}\\ &=& \sum_x \left( x^2 \cdot p(x) -2 \mu x \cdot p(x) + \mu^2 \cdot p(x) \right) & \text{(distributing p(x))}\\ &=& {\color{blue}{\sum_x \left( x^2 \cdot p(x) \right)}} - \sum_x \left(2 \mu x \cdot p(x) \right) + \sum_x \left( \mu^2 \cdot p(x) \right) & \text{(properties of summation)}\\ &=& {\color{blue}{E(X^2)}} - \sum_x \left({\color{red}{2 \mu}} x \cdot p(x) \right) + \sum_x \left( {\color{red}{\mu^2}} \cdot p(x) \right) & \text{(definition of } E(X^2) \text{)}\\ &=& E(X^2) - {\color{red}{2 \mu}} {\color{blue}{\sum_x \left(x \cdot p(x) \right)}} + {\color{red}{\mu^2}} \sum_x p(x) & \text{(prop. of summation)}\\ &=& E(X^2) - 2 \mu {\color{blue}{E(X)}} + + \mu^2 {\color{red}{\sum_x p(x)}} & \text{(definition of } E(X) \text{)} \\ &=& E(X^2) - 2 {\color{blue}{\mu^2}} + \mu^2 \cdot {\color{red}{1}} & \text{(prop. of pmf's)} \\ &=& E(X^2) - \mu^2 & \text{(algebra)} \\ \end{array}\]

Therefore, we see that \(\text{Var}(X) = E(X^2) - \mu^2\).




Comparing Two or More Random Variables

Let \(X\) and \(Y\) denote two random variables (either both discrete or both continuous). The joint probability distribution is a multivariate function denoted \(p(x,y)\) or \(f(x,y)\) that describes the behavior of two (or more) random variables simultaneously.

  • If \(X\) and \(Y\) are discrete, \(p(a,b) = P(X = a \cap Y = b)\).
  • If \(X\) and \(Y\) are continuous, we can use \(f(x,y)\) to compute probabilities as follows: \[P \big( (a < X < b) \cap (c < Y < d) \big) = \int_c^d \int_a^b f(x,y) \, dx \, dy = \int_a^b \int_c^d f(x,y) \, dy \, dx.\]

A joint probability distribution can be used to understand how likely different combinations of these variables are to occur and if there is a relation between the variables.

Marginal Distributions

A marginal distribution function of \(X\) is denoted \(p_X(x)\) or \(f_X(x)\) and gives the probability \(X\) takes certain values, independent of the values of \(Y\). The marginal distribution of \(X\) is derived from the joint probability distribution as follows:

\[p_X(x) = P(X=x) = \sum_{y} p(x,y) \quad \text{or} \quad f_X(x) = \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} f(x,y) \, dy.\]

Likewise, we can find the marginal distribution function for \(Y\):

\[p_Y(y) = P(Y=y) = \sum_{x} p(x,y) \quad \text{or} \quad f_Y(y) = \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} f(x,y) \, dx.\]

Independent Random Variables

Informally, we say two random variables \(X\) and \(Y\) are independent random variables if the value of one has no effect on the value of the other. More formally, if \(X\) and \(Y\) denote two random variables with joint distribution \(f(x,y)\), then \(X\) and \(Y\) are independent if and only if

\[f(x,y) = f_X(x) f_Y(y) , \quad \text{for all } (x,y) \text{ in the domain of } f.\]

If \(X\) and \(Y\) are two independent random variables and \(a\) and \(b\) are two constants, then the following special properties hold:

Properties of Independent Random Variables

  • \(E(XY) = E(X) E(Y)\)

  • \(\text{Var}(aX + bY) = a^2 \text{Var}(X) + b^2 \text{Var}(Y)\)

  • \(\text{Cov}(X,Y) = 0\) (more on this in a second)

Warning

We cannot use any of the properties listed in the bullets above if \(X\) and \(Y\) are dependent random variables.

Question 4

Let random variables \(X\) and \(Y\) denote the education level (in years) and income (in dollars), respectively, of a randomly selected adult.

  • Do you believe \(X\) and \(Y\) are independent random variables? Why or why not?
  • If a person is has a lot of education (say an MS degree), then what would you expect the sign of \(x-\mu_X\) to be? The sign of \(y-\mu_Y\)?
  • If a person has less education (say did not complete HS), then what would you expect the sign of \(x-\mu_X\) to be? The sign of \(y-\mu_Y\)?
  • What would you expect the sign of the product \((x-\mu_X)(y-\mu_Y)\) to be?

Solution to Question 4

  • No, the level of education is associated with higher income earnings.
  • Both \(x-\mu_X\) and \(y-\mu_Y\) would be positive since their education and income would be better than average.
  • Both \(x-\mu_X\) and \(y-\mu_Y\) would be negative since their education and income would be below than average.
  • Thus, the \((x-\mu_X)(y-\mu_Y)\) will be positive (most of the time).




Covariance

The covariance of random variables \(X\) and \(Y\) measures how strong is the dependence between two variables and is denoted \(\text{Cov}(X,Y)\). The covariance is defined using the formula,

\[\text{Cov}(X,Y) = E\bigg( (X-\mu_X)(Y-\mu_Y) \bigg) .\]

  • If \(\text{Cov}(X,Y) > 0\) increasing \(X\) leads to larger values of \(Y\).
    • We say \(X\) and \(Y\) have a positive association.
  • If \(\text{Cov}(X,Y) < 0\) increasing \(X\) leads to smaller values of \(Y\).
    • We say \(X\) and \(Y\) have a negative association.
  • If \(X\) and \(Y\) are independent, then \(\text{Cov}(X,Y) = 0\).
Caution

\(\text{Cov}(X,Y) = 0\) does not always imply that \(X\) and \(Y\) are independent. It is true that if \(X\) and \(Y\) are independent, then \(\text{Cov}(X,Y) = 0\), but the converse is not true. It is possible that \(\text{Cov}(X,Y) = 0\), but \(X\) and \(Y\) are dependent.

Let \(X\) and \(Y\) denote two random variables and \(a\) and \(b\) two constants, then the following properties hold:

Properties of Covariance

  • \(\text{Cov}(X, a) = 0\)

  • \(\text{Cov}(X, X) = \text{Var}(X) = \sigma^2_X\)

  • \(\text{Cov}(X, Y) = \text{Cov}(Y, X)\)

  • \(\text{Cov}(aX, bY) = ab \ \text{Cov}(X,Y)\)

  • \(\text{Cov}(X + a, Y + b) = \text{Cov}(X, Y)\)

  • \(\text{Cov}(X,Y) = E(XY) = E(X)E(Y)\)

Question 5

For any two random variables \(X\) and \(Y\), prove \(\text{Cov}(X,Y) = E(XY) = E(X)E(Y)\).

Solution to Question 5

We start with the definition of covariance and expected value and distributing terms inside the integral. Then we apply properties of integrals and break up sums and pull out multiplication by constants in the work below.

\[\begin{align} \text{Cov}(X,Y) &= E\big( (X-\mu_X)(Y-\mu_Y) \big) \\ &= \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} (x-\mu_x)(y-\mu_Y) f(x,y) \, dx \, dy \\ &= \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} \big( xy f(x,y) + \mu_X \mu_Y f(x,y) - x \mu_Y f(x,y) - y \mu_X f(x,y) \big) \, dx \, dy\\ &= \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} \big( xy f(x,y) \big) \, dx \, dy + \mu_X \mu_Y \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} f(x,y) \, dx \, dy \\ & \ \ \ \ \ - \mu_Y \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} x f(x,y) \, dx \, dy - \mu_X \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} y f(x,y) \bigg) \, dx \, dy\\ \end{align}\]

Next, we recall the following from probability:

  • By definition of expected value, \(\displaystyle \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} \big( xy f(x,y) \big) \, dx \, dy = E(XY)\)
  • By properties of probability distributions, we know definition \(\displaystyle \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} f(x,y) \, dx \, dy = 1\).

Using the two observations above and the fact \(x\) is treated like a constant when we integrate by \(y\), and likewise \(y\) is treated like a constant when we integrate by \(x\), we simplify further. Not one of the double integrals we reverse the order of integration.

\[\begin{align} \text{Cov}(X,Y) &= \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} \big( xy f(x,y) \big) \, dx \, dy + \mu_X \mu_Y \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} f(x,y) \, dx \, dy \\ & \ \ \ \ \ - \mu_Y \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} x f(x,y) \, dx \, dy - \mu_X \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} y f(x,y) \bigg) \, dx \, dy \\ &= E(XY) + \mu_X \mu_Y - \mu_Y \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} x \left( \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} f(x,y) \, dy \right) \, dx - \mu_x \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} y \left( \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} f(x,y) \, dx \right) \, dy \\ &= E(XY) + E(X)E(Y) - E(X) \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} y f_Y(y) \, dy - E(Y) \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} x f_X(x) \, dx \end{align}\]

In the last line of work above, we use the definition of marginal distribution:

  • \(\displaystyle f_X(x) = \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} f(x,y) \, dy\), and
  • \(\displaystyle f_Y(y) = \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} f(x,y) \, dx\).

Lastly, we apply the definition of expected value \(E(X)\) and \(E(Y)\) and simplify.

\[\begin{align} \text{Cov}(X,Y) &= E(XY) + E(X)E(Y) - E(X) \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} y f_Y(y) \, dy - E(Y) \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} x f_X(x) \, dx \\ &= E(XY) + E(X)E(Y) - E(X)E(Y) - E(Y)E(X) \\ &= E(XY) - E(X)E(Y). \end{align}\]

This concludes the proof.

Question 7

Which variable has the biggest positive covariance with earnings (excluding earnings itself)? Which variable has the most negative covariance with earnings? Which variable has the covariance with earnings that is closest to 0? Interpret these observations in practical terms.

Solution to Question 7

The variable hours has the largest covariance with earnings. This makes sense since the more hours a person works, typically the more they earn.

The variable intnum has the most negative covariance with earnings. This does not make too much sense on the surface since intnum seems to be some sort of ID number assigned to households in the 60’s. I would expect the ID to not be associated with earnings either way, but perhaps there is some characteristics that are associated with both the intnum and earnings based on how ID’s were determined?

The variable age has covariance with earnings that is closest to 0. This is a little surprising to me since I’d think as age increases, so do earnings, and that would be a strong association. The value is positive, hinting at a positive association, but not as strong as others.

Question 8

Which variable has correlation with earnings that is closest to \(1\) (excluding earnings itself)? Which variable has correlation with earnings that is closest to \(-1\) ? Which variable has correlation with earnings that is closest to \(0\) ? Interpret these observations in practical terms. How do the compare with your answers to Question 7?

Solution to Question 8

The variable hours also has the correlation with earnings. This makes sense since the more hours a person works, typically the more they earn.

The variable intnum also has the most negative correlation with earnings. Again, as stated in the previous question, this might seem odd on the surface without knowing what intnum is capturing in the ID (if anything)

The variable persnum has correlation value with earnings that is closest to 0 which is different from the covariance, cov(age, earnings), was closest to zero. This makes a little more sense since I would expect the earnings to be independent from persnum which is an ID assigned (at random?).

Based on the previous question, the variable with the correlation coefficient closest to 1 with earnings and hours. Thus, we choose hours as our predictor and earnings as the response variable.

A First Look at Linear Regression in R

We can use the base R function lm(y ~ x , data = df) find estimates for the coefficients, denoted \(\hat{beta}_0\) and \(\hat{\beta}_1\), in linear regression model of the form \(y = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x\). Run ?lm from the console to learn more.

lmod <- lm(earnings ~ hours, data = PSID)
summary(lmod)

Call:
lm(formula = earnings ~ hours, data = PSID)

Residuals:
   Min     1Q Median     3Q    Max 
-52477  -5660   -999   1987 217021 

Coefficients:
            Estimate Std. Error t value Pr(>|t|)    
(Intercept) 999.4906   291.2004   3.432 0.000603 ***
hours        10.7218     0.1871  57.313  < 2e-16 ***
---
Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1

Residual standard error: 12350 on 4854 degrees of freedom
Multiple R-squared:  0.4036,    Adjusted R-squared:  0.4035 
F-statistic:  3285 on 1 and 4854 DF,  p-value: < 2.2e-16

From the summary output above, we see the linear relation is statistically significant with an extremely small p-value (2.2e-16). A 95% confidence interval for the slope is approximately \(10.7218 \pm 1.96 (0.1871)\) which contains only positive values which is why the result is statistically significant. The linear model that best fits the data is

\[\widehat{\text{earnings}} = 999.4906 + 10.7218 \cdot \widehat{\text{hours}}\]

The error of the predicted values are called the residuals.

From the plot above, we might infer our model is biased in the sense it gives some very large overestimates, but the underestimates are not as drastic.

The predict() function is used to make predictions based on results of various model fitting functions, lm() being of such model fitting function.

# prediction corresponding to hours values stored in new_data

Question 10: Practice with Joint Distributions

A large insurance agency services a number of customers who have purchased both a homeowner’s policy and an automobile policy from the agency. For each type of policy, a deductible amount must be specified. For an automobile policy, the choices are \(\$100\) and \(\$250\), whereas for a homeowner’s policy, the choices are \(\$0\), \(\$100\), and \(\$200\).

Suppose an individual with both types of policy is selected at random from the agency’s files. Let \(A\) be the deductible amount on the auto policy and \(H\) the deductible amount on the homeowner’s policy. The joint probability mass function for \(A\) and \(H\) is denoted \(p(a,h)=P(A=a \mbox{ and } H=h)\) and is summarized in the two-way table below.


  • Interpret the meaning of the value \(p(100,0)=0.2\) in this context.
  • Write piecewise formulas for \(p_A(a)\) and \(p_H(h)\) and interpret their values.
  • Are random variables \(A\) and \(H\) independent? Explain.
  • Compute \(\text{Cov}(A, H)\).

Solution to Question 10

Interpreting Joint Probability Mass Functions

\(p(100, 0) = 0.2\) means 20% of customers have an auto deductible of \(\$100\) and no deductible for home insurance.

Finding and Interpreting Marginal Distributions

By definition, we can find the marginal distribution of \(A\) as follows:

\[\begin{align} p_A (100) &= \sum_h p(100, h) = 0.20 + 0.10 + 0.2 = 0.5 \\ p_A (250) &= \sum_h p(100, h) = 0.20 + 0.10 + 0.2 = 0.5 \end{align}\]

Practically speaking, this means half of the customers have a \(\$100\) auto deductible and the other half have a \(\$250\) auto deductible. Their customers are equally likely to choose any one of the two options for their auto deductible.

We can express the marginal distribution of \(A\) as the piecewise function below.

\[p_A(a) = \left\{ \begin{array}{ll} 0.5 & a=100 \\ 0.5 & a=250 \\ 0 & \mbox{otherwise} \end{array} \right.\]

Similarly, we have the marginal distribution of \(H\) which we compute by essentially calculating the column total for each value of \(H\).

\[p_H(h) = \left\{ \begin{array}{ll} 0.25 & h=0 \\ 0.25 & h=100 \\ 0.5 & h=200 \\ 0 & \mbox{otherwise} \end{array} \right.\]

One quarter of their customers chose a home owners policy with no deductible, one quarter chose a \(\$100\) home deductible, and the remaining 50% chose a \(\$200\) home deductible.

Independence?

We can first think about this intuitively, and then do some math to see if our intuition lines up with the data. The two variables are likely to be dependent since we expect (maybe) a person who chooses a higher auto deductible to also choose a higher home deductible. Conversely, a person who chooses a lower auto deductible to also choose a lower home deductible. We should not claim there is a casual relation, just some association between the two. There are likely confounding variables that effect the deductible amounts people choose such as possibly risk aversion, socioeconomic status, age, gender, and race to new some.

Let’s do the math. By definition, to random variables are independent if and only if

\[p(a, h) = p_A(a) p_H(h) \quad \text{for all } (a, h) \text{ in the domain of } p(a,h).\]

Let’s consider the point \((100, 0)\) in the domain of \(p(a, h)\). We have

  • \(p(100,0) = 0.2\)
  • \(p_A(100) p_H(0) = (0.5)(0.25) = 0.125\)
  • \(p(100,0) \ne p_A(100) p_H(0)\)

We have identified one point where \(p(a, h) = p_A(a) p_H(h)\) which is enough to show \(A\) and \(H\) are dependent random variables. To confirm they are independent, we would need to show \(p(a, h) = p_A(a) p_H(h)\) for all possible pairs \((a, h)\) in the table.

Calculating Covariance

Since we have already found \(p_A(a)\) and \(P_H(h)\), we compute \(E(X)\), \(E(Y)\), and \(E(XY)\) and use the property \(\text{Cov}(X,Y) = E(XY) - E(X)E(Y)\).

\[\begin{align} E(A) &= \sum_A (a \cdot p_A(a)) = (100) (0.5) + 250 (0.5) = 175\\ E(H) &= \sum_H (h \cdot p_H(h)) = (0)(0.25) + (100) (0.25) + (200) (0.5) = 125\\ \end{align}\]

The average of the auto deductibles is \(\$175\) (though that is not an option for any single person to select), and the average of the home deductibles is \(\$125\) (which is also not an option for any one person).

Next we compute the expected value of the product of the deductible values \(ah\). This does not really have practical significance in this context.

\[\begin{align} E(AH) &= \sum_{(a,h)} \bigg( (ah) \cdot p(a,h) \bigg)\\ &= (100 \cdot 0)p(100, 0) + (100 \cdot 100) p(100,100) + (100 \cdot 200) p(100,200) + \ldots + (250 \cdot 200) p(250, 200) \\ &= 23,\!750 \end{align}\]

From these calculations, we have

\[\text{Cov}(A, H) = E(AH) - E(A)E(H) = 23,\!750 - (175)(125) = 1,\!875\]

The covariance is positive which lines up with our initial intuition.

exp_ah <- 100 * 0 * 0.2 + 
  100 * 100 * 0.1 + 
  100 * 200 * 0.2 + 
  250 * 0 * 0.05 +
  250 * 100 * 0.15 + 
  250 * 200 * 0.3

exp_ah
[1] 23750
cov_ah <- exp_ah - 175 * 125
cov_ah
[1] 1875




Appendix A: Common Discrete Random Variables

The Binomial Distribution

\(X \sim \text{Binom}(n,p)\) is number of successes from \(n\) identical and independent trials each with probability of success \(p\).

\[f(x; n, p) = \left\{ \begin{array}{ll} \left( \begin{array}{c} n\\ x \end{array} \right) p^x(1-p)^{n-x} \ \ & \text{for } x =0,1,2, \ldots , n\\ & \\ 0 \ \ & \text{otherwise} \end{array} \right.\]

  • The expected value is \(E(X) = \mu_X = np\).
  • The variance is \(\text{Var} (X) = \sigma_X^2 = np(1-p)\).
  • Use dbinom(x, n, p) to calculate \(p(x) = P(X = x)\).
  • Use pbinom(x, n, p) to calculate \(F(x) = P(X \leq x)\).
  • Use rbinom(m, n, p) to generate a random sample of size \(m\) from population \(X \sim \text{Binom}(n,p)\).
  • Use qbinom(q, n, p) to find the qth percentile of \(X \sim \text{Binom}(n,p)\).

The Discrete Uniform Distribution

There are \(k\) distinct outcomes each with an equal likelihood of occurring.

\[f(x; k) = \left\{ \begin{array}{ll} \dfrac{1}{k} \ \ & \text{for } x = 1, 2, \ldots, k\\ 0 \ \ & \text{otherwise} \end{array} \right.\]

  • The expected value is \(\displaystyle E(X) = \mu_X = \frac{k+1}{2}\).
  • The variance is \(\displaystyle \text{Var} (X) = \sigma_X^2 = \frac{k^2-1}{12}\).
  • Note functions such as dunif(), punif(), runif(), and qunif() are for the continuous (not discrete) uniform distribution.
  • It is typically easier to calculate probabilities directly rather than use technology.

The Geometric Distribution

\(X \sim \text{Geom}(p)\) is the number of failures that occur before the first success, where \(p\) denotes the probability of a success and \(q=1-p\) is the probability of a failure.

\[f(x; p) = \left\{ \begin{array}{ll} q^xp \ \ & \text{for } x = 0, 1, 2, \ldots \\ 0 & \text{otherwise} \end{array} \right. .\]

  • The expected value is \(E(X) = \mu_X = \dfrac{q}{p}\).
  • The variance is \(\text{Var} (X) = \sigma_X^2 = \dfrac{q}{p^2}\).
  • Use dgeom(x, p) to calculate \(p(x) = P(X = x)\).
  • Use pgeom(x, p) to calculate \(F(x) = P(X \leq x)\).
  • Use rgeom(m, p) to generate a random sample of size \(m\) from population \(X \sim \text{Geom}(p)\).
  • Use qgeom(q, p) to find the qth percentile of \(X \sim \text{Geom}(p)\).

The Poisson Distribution

\(X \sim \text{Pois}(\lambda)\) is the number of times an event occurs in a fixed time period, where \(\lambda\) denotes the mean number of occurrences in the given time period.

\[f(x; \lambda) = \left\{ \begin{array}{ll} e^{-\lambda} \dfrac{\lambda^x}{x!} \ \ & \text{for } x = 0, 1, 2, \ldots \\ 0 & \text{otherwise} \end{array} \right. .\]

  • The expected value is \(E(X) = \mu_X = \lambda\).
  • The variance is \(\text{Var} (X) = \sigma_X^2 = \lambda\).
  • Use dpois(x, lambda) to calculate \(p(x) = P(X = x)\).
  • Use ppois(x, lambda) to calculate \(F(x) = P(X \leq x)\).
  • Use rpois(m, lambda) to generate a random sample of size \(m\) from population \(X \sim \text{Pois}(\lambda)\).
  • Use qpois(q, lambda) to find the qth percentile of \(X \sim \text{Pois}(\lambda)\).

Appendix B: Common Continuous Random Variables

Normal Distributions

If \(X\) is normally distributed with mean \(\mu\) and standard deviation \(\sigma\), we write \(\color{dodgerblue}{X \sim N( \mu ,\sigma)}\). The formula for the probability density is called the Gaussian and is given below.

\[f(x; \mu, \sigma) = \dfrac{1}{\sigma\sqrt{2\pi}} e^{-\frac{1}{2} \left( \frac{x-\mu}{\sigma} \right)^2}\]

  • The expected value is \(E(X) = \mu\).
  • The variance is \(\text{Var} (X) = \sigma^2\).
  • Use dnorm(x, mu, sigma) to calculate \(f(x)\).
    • Recall for continuous distributions, \(f(x)\) gives the height of the pdf.
    • Probabilities are areas under \(f(x)\) (not the heights).
    • DO NOT use dnorm() to compute probabilities.
  • Use pnorm(x, mu, sigma) to calculate \(P(X \leq x)\), the area to the left of \(X=x\).
    • One last warning, be sure to use pnorm() to compute probabilities not dnorm().
  • Use rnorm(n, mu, sigma) to generate a random sample of size \(n\) from population \(X \sim N(mu, sigma)\).
  • Use qnorm(q, mu, sigma) to find the qth percentile.
  • We have the 68%-95%-99.5% Empirical Rule.
  • We can standardize the normal distribution using z-scores: \[z = \frac{x - \mu}{\sigma}\]

Continuous Uniform Distributions

\(X\) is a continuous uniform distribution when \(X\) is equally likely to equal to any value on the closed, continuous interval \(\lbrack a , b \rbrack\). If a continuous random variable is uniformly distributed on the interval \(\lbrack a , b \rbrack\), the pdf is

\[f(x; a,b) = \left\{ \begin{array}{ll} \dfrac{1}{b-a} & a \leq x \leq b\\ 0 & \text{otherwise} \end{array} \right. .\]

The corresponding cdf is

\[F(x) = \left\{ \begin{array}{ll} 0, & x<a \\ \frac{x-a}{b-a}, & a \leq x \leq b \\ 1, & x>b \end{array} \right. .\]

  • The expected value is \(E(X) = \dfrac{a+b}{2}\)
  • The variance is \(\text{Var}(X) = \dfrac{(b-a)^2}{12}\)

When working with uniform distributions, it is typically easier to calculate probabilities “by hand” without the need for technology. However, R does have functions to help!

  • Use dunif(x, a, b) to find the height of the pdf function, which is \(\frac{1}{b-a}\).
    • There is really no need to use the function since the pdf has a constant height.
    • DO NOT use dunif() to compute probabilities.
  • Use punif(x, a, b) to calculate \(P(X \leq x)=\int_a^x \frac{1}{b-a} \, dt = \frac{x-a}{b-a}\).
    • Probabilities can be found by computing areas of rectangles which may be easier!
  • Use runif(n, a, b) to generate a random sample of size \(n\) from population \(X \sim \text{Unif}(a, b)\).
  • Use qunif(q, a, b) to find the qth percentile.

Exponential Distributions

Let \(X\) be the amount of time between the successive events if we know the average time between occurrences is \(\mu\). The rate parameter \(\lambda = \frac{1}{\mu}\) is the average number of times the event occurs per unit of time. Then \(X\) is exponentially distributed with rate parameter \(\lambda\), and we write \(\color{dodgerblue}{X \sim \text{Exp} (\lambda)}\).

The pdf for \(X \sim \text{Exp} (\lambda)\) is the exponential function

\[f(x; \lambda) = \lambda e^{-\lambda x} \quad \text{for } x >0 .\]

  • The expected value is \(E(X) = \dfrac{1}{\lambda}=\mu\)
  • The variance is \(\text{Var}(X) = \dfrac{1}{\lambda^2} = \mu^2\).
  • Use dexp(x, lambda) to find the height of the pdf function, which is \(\lambda e^{-\lambda x}\).
    • DO NOT use dexp() to compute probabilities.
  • Use pexp(x, lambda) to calculate \(P(X \leq x)=\int_0^x \lambda e^{-\lambda t} \, dt\).
    • It never hurts to practice your integration and check with pexp()!
  • Use rexp(n, lambda) to generate a random sample of size \(n\) from population \(X \sim \text{Exp}(\lambda)\).
  • Use qexp(q, lambda) to find the qth percentile.

Gamma Distributions

A gamma distribution is a distribution that arises naturally in processes for which the waiting times between events are relevant. Suppose we know that \(\mu\) is the mean amount of time between successive occurrences of an event. Let \(X\) be the amount of time it takes for the event to occur \(r\) times.

  • The rate parameter \(\color{dodgerblue}{\lambda = \frac{1}{\mu}}\) tells us how many times an event occurs per unit of time.
  • The shape parameter \(\color{dodgerblue}{r}\) denotes the total number of occurrences we will wait to occur.

Then \(X\) will follow a gamma distribution that we denote \(\color{dodgerblue}{X \sim \text{Gamma} ( r, \lambda)}\). The pdf is given by

\[f(x;r, \lambda) = \frac{1}{(r-1)!} \lambda^r x^{r-1} e^{-\lambda x} \quad \text{for } x >0 .\]

  • The expected value is \(E(X) = \dfrac{r}{\lambda}\)
  • The variance is \(\text{Var}(X) = \dfrac{r}{\lambda^2}\).
  • Use dgamma(x, r, lambda) to find the height of the pdf function which is generally not too useful.
    • DO NOT use dgamma() to compute probabilities.
  • Use pgamma(x, r, lambda) to calculate \(P(X \leq x)\).
  • Use rgamma(n, r, lambda) to generate a random sample of size \(n\) from population \(X \sim \text{Gamma}(r, \lambda)\).
  • Use qgamma(q, r, lambda) to find the qth percentile.
